title: Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Note: This exhibition is held in the Leventhal Map and Education Gallery which is open Tuesday 11am-5pm, Wednesday 1pm-7pm, Thursday - Saturday 11am - 5pm, Sunday 1pm - 5pm. Please check their website for the most up to date hours and schedule.Maps trace out the complicated history of places, and we can use them to document geography in much the same way that we can use diaries and letters to document biography. In the eight cases of this exhibition, we follow the changing spatial forms of the place we now call Boston—from before the landscape carried that name all the way through the struggles, clashes, and dreams that continue to reshape the city today. These maps don’t merely depict facts about how the city looked at different moments in its history. Instead, they invite us to contemplate how geographic forces, both natural and human, have constructed the physical and social world around us, through large and small transformations that have transpired over many centuries. The Leventhal Map & Education Center regularly mounts exhibitions in our gallery, located in the historic McKim Building in the Boston Public Library in Copley Square. All of our exhibitions feature scholarly research as well as activities for families, children, and educators. Our permanent exhibit, Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City, is available any time our public gallery is open. Visit the digital exhibition to Becoming Boston here. title: Declarations: Printing a New Nation
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Note: This exhibition is held in the Leventhal Map and Education Gallery which is open Tuesday 11am-5pm, Wednesday 1pm-7pm, Thursday - Saturday 11am - 5pm, Sunday 1pm - 5pm. Please check their website for the most up to date hours and schedule. On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress ratified the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia. The next day, the first printed copies were sent off and began to circulate throughout the thirteen colonies, which were now, on paper, independent states. Throughout July and August of 1776, the Declaration was reprinted in major American cities and small towns alike. Some of these new printings appeared in newspapers. Others were issued as large, single-sheet publications known as broadsides. Many versions, in both formats, were printed before the delegates to the Continental Congress began to sign the official handwritten Declaration in early August. These early printings of the Declaration were created at a time when the independence of the future United States was anything but certain. From the perspective of those who read it in the summer of 1776, we can see the Declaration of Independence in its original form: not yet a famous founding document, but breaking news. In the exhibition Declarations: Printing a New Nation, see eight different original printings of the Declaration of Independence, and take a journey that explores how the news of independence spread out from Philadelphia in the summer of 1776 when the ink was not yet dry on the founding documents of a new nation. title: Lexicon
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] July 2026Aluminum · 18 × 18 × 2 ftAlfonso Parra Rubio · Erik StrandMIT Center for Bits and Atoms Lexicon is a free-form structural shell built from individual origami-folded cells assembled into a two-sided lattice, or interlocking framework. The folding and assembling process creates a structure that is as strong and rigid as typical building methods, but it is much lighter. The structure is made for this space, Deferrari Hall. Its light, curved shape contrasts with the Boylston Street Building's heavy and blocky brutalist architecture. Lexicon's three pointed shape is a reference to Rafael Guastavino's tiled ceilings in the Central Library's McKim Building. By bringing together influences from both of the Central Library's buildings, Lexicon celebrates the role of geometry in design and construction. A collaboration between the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the Boston Public Library (BPL), and the Mayor's Office of Arts and Culture (MOAC). With Riccardo Foschi (University of Bologna), Rupert Malec (University of Innsbruck), Tomohiro Tachi (University of Tokyo), and Neil Gershenfeld (MIT Center for Bits and Atoms). Made possible and funded by MOAC.

title: Paper Folding Craft: Crease, Fold, Transform
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for this introductory talk followed by a drop-in activity for all ages! Folding is everywhere and in all scales! From how a leaf packs inside a bud, how a protein takes form, how a satellite stows for launch, and how a single sheet of paper becomes a structure that stands on its own. We will begin with a short presentation that traces this story. Folding is something inherent to nature, and we humans have long used it as a tool. Over time that tool became a craft, the craft became an art, and the art became a science. As an example of where all of this leads, we will then move into a hands-on activity. In this workshop, participants of all ages will explore the science and art of folding using nothing but their own hands. No experience needed. In this workshop, participants will: Discover the transformational power of folding, by turning flat sheets into strong, three dimensional forms. Explore the geometry hiding inside everyday folds. Work with a single unit cell and discover how the same building block can be folded and combined into many different shapes. Build something to take home. The heart of the workshop is to invite people to be curious with their hands, with a simple but surprising idea: given the same unit cell, no two people have to arrive at the same shape. Starting from identical pieces, participants will fold and assemble their own polyhedra, comparing the many forms that emerge from one shared starting point. title: Handwriting the Constitution and Declaration of Independence
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] In honor of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, visitors are invited to handwrite the Declaration and the US Constitution in the Courtyard of the Central Library in Copley Square. This program aims to create time and a quiet space to reflect and deepen one's understanding of these historic documents. All supplies will be provided. Participants will first stop by the supply table to pick up writing supplies and copies of the Constitution and/or Declaration of Independence. Reproductions of John Adams's personal copy of the Constitution held by Special Collections will also be available to transcribe. This program is self-paced. Patrons are invited to stay for the whole session or simply stay as long as they would like. About Handwriting the Constitution Handwriting the Constitution is a social art project begun in 2017 by artist Morgan O'Hara. It invites people from all walks of life to meet in public spaces to handwrite the US Constitution or other documents written to protect human rights and freedoms. This art practice was created so that people will know their rights, deepen their understanding of laws created to protect these rights, and to help resist negative thinking. The goal of this art practice is to encourage people to hold their own Handwriting sessions on a recurring basis; to create a physical and psychological space that explores the practice of concentrated writing as an art form, and a process designed to bring people together in a quiet and calming way, all by focusing on human rights. It has been identified as a powerful and transformative form of activism for introverts. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. Through interactive, hands-on workshops, students will explore creative industries while building confidence, teamwork, and innovation skills in a fun and supportive environment. About Future Creators & Innovators (FCI) Future Creators & Innovators (FCI) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded in 2023 by Rebekah Israel while she was a student at Miami Dade College. What began as a passion for helping young people explore their potential has grown into a community-focused organization dedicated to career exploration, creativity, leadership development, and hands-on learning experiences. Now a student at Emerson College, Rebekah continues to lead FCI's mission of connecting students with professionals, mentors, and real-world opportunities that inspire confidence and future success. As the organization has expanded, Rebekah recruited Sophia Lam to serve as Director of Programs & Outreach. Sophia is an Emerson College graduate with a Bachelor of Science in Communication Studies and minors in Public Relations and Nonprofit Communication Management. Together, they work to create engaging educational experiences that empower youth to discover their strengths, develop new skills, and explore future career pathways. title: Author Talk: Dr. Tiffany Joseph - Not All In: Race, Immigration, and Healthcare Exclusion in the Age of Obamacare
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Sociologist Tiffany Joseph discusses her 2025 non-fiction book, Not All In: Race, Immigration, and Healthcare Exclusion in the Age of Obamacare as she leads a talk exposing a troubling paradox at the heart of Massachusetts' celebrated health care system. Even in a state long held up as a model of reform, immigrants' race, ethnicity, and legal status still shape who gets real access to coverage and care. Drawing on nearly a decade of research in Boston's Brazilian, Dominican, and Salvadoran communities, Joseph traces how the promise of the Massachusetts and Affordable Care Act health reforms collided with the lived realities of immigrant patients. As new federal cuts to health coverage and the social safety net take hold, Joseph's research offers a lens for understanding an exclusion that once targeted immigrants and now reaches citizens too. Dr. Tiffany Joseph is Professor of Sociology and International Affairs Program at Northeastern University. Her research and teaching interests explore race, ethnicity, and migration in the Americas and healthcare access in the United States. Her most recent book, Not All In: Race, Immigration, and Healthcare Exclusion in the Age of Obamacare (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2025), explores how documentation status, race, and ethnicity influence the healthcare access of immigrants after comprehensive health reform. She has received grants and awards from the Ford Foundation, Institute for Citizens and Scholars, Institute for International Education Fulbright Program, National Institutes of Health, National Science Foundation, and Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. She is also the author of Race on the Move: Brazilian Migrants and the Global Reconstruction of Race (Stanford University Press, 2015) and her work has been published in various peer reviewed journals and national media outlets. title: College Essay Basic Training: What High School Seniors Need to Know - 2-Session In-Person Workshop [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] NOTE: This is a 2-session in-person workshop. Attendees will need access to Google Classroom using a non-school Gmail account to make full use of these tools. In-person attendees will be provided computer access, but may choose to use their own device. Each year, millions of high-school seniors compose a 650-word essay for the Common Application. Before clicking "Submit," too many of them sit idle by their computer screen, waiting hours for the perfect idea to strike them as they struggle to shake off those all-too-common anxieties: What am I supposed to write about...? How do I write an essay about myself...? What if there's nothing special about me...? This 2-session seminar will walk high-school seniors through the DOs and DON'Ts of the Common Application essay, using a variety of strategies to help students think first about what they want colleges to know about them, and second about how to show that through effective, candid narration. Through studying a variety of models, students will learn a set of techniques and approaches to make their story honest, revealing, and memorable; a variety of writing exercises and live commentary from trained, qualified library staff will give them tools necessary to end the course with the beginnings of a working draft (or more!). title: Starting and Growing a Business: The SBA Advantage
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you thinking of Starting a Business? Do you need small business assistance? The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) can help! Join Shelly Gillis, Outreach and Marketing Specialist with the SBA in the Massachusetts District Office, to learn how their programs and services can help your business. This workshop aims to provide you with a better understanding of the various programs and services offered by the SBA that are available to prospective or current entrepreneurs who need assistance in starting or expanding their businesses. We’ll cover: An overview of the SBA and its Resource Partner NetworkHow the SBDC, CWE, VBOC and SCORE can help through business training and 1:1 mentoringAccessing capital SBA-backed loan programs Let the Small Business Administration (SBA), help you get “procurement-ready” to market your firm’s products and services to the Federal Government through our Resource Partners Network. Federal Government Contracting can represent a very profitable market for your business — but it can also be extremely complex to get started and thrive. The SBA and its resource partners can help you determine if your business is ready for federal contracting by assessing your business for: Marketability​Structure and experience​Systems and capacityAbility to find contracts Shelly Gillis is an Outreach and Marketing Specialist with the Small Business Administration Massachusetts District Office. She’s passionate about supporting small businesses and entrepreneurs in the Commonwealth by connecting them with community partners and resources. Formerly with for the US Census Bureau for 13 years, she was involved in both field operations and Decennial Census promotion in the Boston area. She has a background in sales and marketing, having worked as an award-winning sales representative and sales manager with Entertainment Publications in Massachusetts. Ms. Gillis holds a master’s degree in education from UMass Boston and a Bachelor of Journalism degree from the University of Nebraska with an advertising major. She is a proud Boston resident for 32 years, but loves her Nebraska roots and is a loyal Cornhusker fan.Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Create It! with Future Creators and Innovators [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The Create It! Workshop Series is a two-week creative arts and media program designed to introduce youth to various forms of artistic expression, digital media, storytelling, and performance arts. Through interactive, hands-on workshops, students will explore creative industries while building confidence, teamwork, and innovation skills in a fun and supportive environment. Teens will engage in workshops focused on content creation, visual arts, photography, filmmaking, branding, theater, and digital editing while learning from guest speakers and creative professionals. Teens can sign up for all 6 workshops as each one builds on the next, or can drop in for the workshops that are most interesting or relevant to them. Day 1: Logo Design & Sticker Creation on CanvaTeens will design custom logos and stickers using Canva while learning the basics of branding, creativity, and graphic design.Day 2: Photography & Visual Storytelling WorkshopTeens will learn photography fundamentals, including lighting, angles, composition, and storytelling through images. Day 3: Theater: Guest Speaker – Victoria Yordt of ArtservatoryTeens will be introduced to theater, stage presence, confidence-building, storytelling, and performing arts career pathways through an engaging guest speaker session.Day 4: Canvas Painting WorkshopA hands-on painting workshop encouraging creative self-expression through visual art, color, and imagination. Day 5: Digital Creator Workshop: Guest Speaker - Mark BrodieIn this workshop, Mark will introduce students to the fundamentals of digital storytelling and show how images, video, sound, and narrative can be combined to create compelling stories that inform, inspire, and engage others.1. Facilitating how to create media with your phone2. Building social presence on social platforms (both professionally and personally)a. Why branding is so important3. Phone Filming Workshop Day 6: Video Editing & Post-Production WorkshopTeens will learn editing basics such as transitions, sound, captions, and post-production techniques to transform raw footage into completed creative projects. About Future Creators & Innovators (FCI) Future Creators & Innovators (FCI) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded in 2023 by Rebekah Israel while she was a student at Miami Dade College. What began as a passion for helping young people explore their potential has grown into a community-focused organization dedicated to career exploration, creativity, leadership development, and hands-on learning experiences. Now a student at Emerson College, Rebekah continues to lead FCI's mission of connecting students with professionals, mentors, and real-world opportunities that inspire confidence and future success. As the organization has expanded, Rebekah recruited Sophia Lam to serve as Director of Programs & Outreach. Sophia is an Emerson College graduate with a Bachelor of Science in Communication Studies and minors in Public Relations and Nonprofit Communication Management. Together, they work to create engaging educational experiences that empower youth to discover their strengths, develop new skills, and explore future career pathways. Guest Speaker - Mark Brodie Mark Brodie is an Executive-in-Residence in the Department of Communication Studies at Emerson College, where he teaches Digital Storytelling, Podcasting, and Nonprofit Communication. His work focuses on how stories can inspire action, build communities, and create positive change. He believes that everyone has a story worth telling and that today's digital tools make it possible for anyone to reach an audience. Guest Speaker - Victoria Artservatorey Victoria is the Founder and Executive Director of Artservatorey, a nonprofit dedicated to expanding access to creative and performing arts programming for children and youth across Massachusetts. She brings more than a decade of experience as both an actor and arts educator. Victoria studied drama at the Professional Performing Arts School in New York City and holds a Master’s of Education in Educational Leadership and Policy from Boston College. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at the Boston Public Library’s Central Library at Copley Square. title: Word on the Street: Conserving National & Personal Histories
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Conservator Katie Boodle from the Northeast Document Conservation Center will hold a talk about her work conserving newspapers, broadsides, and other documents that spread the news of the formation of the United States Government, as well as provide advice on continuing to preserve similar paper formats that document life today.Throughout history, humanity has created many ways to share written stories and ideas with one another. Dissemination of information through print mediums such as newspapers and broadsides increased significantly over time thanks to improved literacy, mechanical printing options, and mass production of materials. While this resulted in wider and more rapid information sharing, repeated use and exposure to the elements that were a natural part of sharing these objects has led to damage throughout the course of their lifetime. In this talk, Senior Conservator Katie Boodle from the Northeast Document Conservation Center will share how conservation treatment and preservation methods help make the newspapers, broadsides, and other documents that spread the news of the formation of the United States Government accessible to the public today. She will also provide advice on how to preserve similar paper formats that may be found in your homes and tell the story of your personal American history. About the Speaker:Katie Boodle is a Senior Conservator at the Northeast Document Conservation Center (NEDCC) in Andover, MA. Throughout her tenure at NEDCC, she has specialized in the treatment of paper- and parchment-based objects from national, state, and personal collections. She earned her M.A. of Art Conservation from the University of the Arts London and has been working in the field of conservation since 2010. title: Diego Herrera: Concerts in the Courtyard Series
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for this Latin R&B music performance as part of our Wednesday evening concerts that feature Berklee College of Music students performing a range of genres. Diego Herrera is a Peruvian saxophonist and composer creating original music that blends Latin genres with contemporary R&B and pop elements, resulting in a fresh, elegant, and highly distinctive sound. His work is an intersection of tradition and modernity, offering a unique fusion that feels both authentic and easy to listen to. In January of this year, Herrera completed his second fully sold-out tour in Peru, further establishing himself as a strong presence within the Latin jazz fusion and instrumental R&B scene. He is currently in his seventh semester at Berklee College of Music, where he continues to refine his sound and develop his vision as a bandleader and composer. His live show and artistic concept invites listeners on a nocturnal journey through the streets, sounds, and traditions of Latin America, presented in an instrumental, romantic, and cinematic way. His project is further enriched through collaborations with vocalists, integrating the human voice as a narrative element within his musical universe. In addition to having music released on major streaming platforms and maintaining a strong social media presence, Herrera actively creates content that documents his life and artistic journey as a Latin American musician studying at Berklee College of Music in Boston. Through vlogs and behind-the-scenes content, some of which have reached 100k+ views, he has been able to connect with and motivate many young Latin artists who aspire to study at Berklee, move to the United States, and pursue a career in music Registration is not required but the limited amount of seating is first come, first served. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us in partnership with the Citywide Friends of the Boston Public Library in person for this hour-long talk with noted psychologist and author Steven Pinker about his latest book, When Everyone Knows That Everyone Knows…. It sounds impossible, but “superlatively gifted science writer” (The Times) Steven Pinker shows that we do it all the time. This awareness, which we experience as something that is public or “out there,” is called common knowledge, and it has a momentous impact on our social, political, and economic lives. Author bio: Steven Pinker is the Johnstone Professor of Psychology at Harvard University. He has won many prizes for his teaching, his research on language, cognition, and social relations, and his twelve books, including The Language Instinct, How the Mind Works, The Better Angels of Our Nature, and Rationality. He is an elected member of the National Academy of Sciences, a two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist, and one of Time’s “100 Most Influential People in the World Today.” Talks for Better Living The City-Wide Friends of the Boston Public Library and the Boston Public Library invite you to a series of talks featuring world class authors. title: Exhibition: Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] To mark the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the Boston Public Library's Community History Department partnered with Revolutionary Spaces to offer a free and public program series called "Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness." Named for the unalienable rights identified in the Declaration—rights that inherently belong to all human beings, and that governments are created to protect—these programs brought people together to explore, question, and find inspiration in the Declaration of Independence. During two printmaking workshops and four declaration writing workshops at the BPL, library visitors reflected on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution. Displayed together, the art prints and writing pieces made by community members speak to the ongoing American struggle to create and sustain a free society. As a viewer of the exhibition, we invite you to consider: How do I identify with this nation's founding document? What do I celebrate? How do I use my voice in protest? About Community History The BPL Community History Department aims to democratize the expression of history by supporting people in their efforts to document the stories of themselves and their communities. We offer resources, programs, and support for local and community history work based on people’s lived experiences, knowledge, and expertise. About Revolutionary Spaces Revolutionary Spaces stewards the historic Old South Meeting House and Old State House as landmarks, museums, and active civic spaces. Its mission is to bring people together to explore the American struggle to create and sustain a free society—using history as a powerful tool for civic engagement and public dialogue. For more information, visit RevolutionarySpaces.org or follow them on social media at @RevSpaces. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Emily Sweeney - Dropkick Murphy : A Legendary Life
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join Boston Globe reporter Emily Sweeney with her authentic Boston accent, for a discussion of her biography of local luminary Dr. John Murphy, aka "Dropkick" Murphy and his life in and outside the wrestling arena. Newspapers called him the “the man with the cast-iron toes,” “the best drop-kicker in wrestling,” and “one of the mat game’s biggest box office attractions.” But Dr. John “Dropkick” Murphy’s legacy extends far beyond the wrestling ring. Decades before the Betty Ford Center became a household name — and long before the band the Dropkick Murphys named themselves in his honor — the phrase going to Dropkick’s meant a person struggling with addiction needed help and would soon get some. This book chronicles for the first time the unbelievable life of Dr. “Dropkick” Murphy, a professional wrestler who put himself through medical school during the Great Depression and then opened Bellows Farm in Acton, MA, a one-of-a-kind institution that served as both a facility where elite athletes could train as well as a secluded place where down-on-their-luck alcoholics could go to sober up discreetly. The celebrities who frequented Dropkick Murphy’s farm were many, and numerous professional athletes would go there to focus on their training and work out in his state-of-the-art gymnasium. As a result, Bellows Farm featured an unrivaled and revolving cast of colorful characters who brought it to life. Drawing on years of research and interviews, author Emily Sweeney goes behind the scenes to reveal the untold story of Murphy’s life, his farm, and the legendary events that unfolded there. Emily Sweeney is a staff reporter at the Boston Globe and author of the books Boston Organized Crime and Gangland Boston. A proud native of Dorchester, she also appears in Bloody Boston, a two-part documentary special on the Reelz channel; Stranger Than Fiction: The True Story of Whitey Bulger, Southie, and The Departed, a bonus feature on the DVD of the Oscar-winning movie The Departed; and the forthcoming Netflix series How To Become A Mob Boss. title: Starting and Growing a Business: The SBA Advantage
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you thinking of Starting a Business? Do you need small business assistance? The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) can help! Join Shelly Gillis, Outreach and Marketing Specialist with the SBA in the Massachusetts District Office to learn how their programs and services can help your business. This workshop aims to provide you with a better understanding of the various programs and services offered by the SBA that are available to prospective or current entrepreneurs who need assistance in starting or expanding their businesses. We’ll cover: An overview of the SBA and its Resource Partner Network How the SBDC, CWE, VBOC and SCORE can help through business training and 1:1 mentoringAccessing capital SBA-backed loan programs Let the Small Business Administration (SBA), help you get “procurement-ready” to market your firm’s products and services to the Federal Government through our Resource Partners Network. Federal Government Contracting can represent a very profitable market for your business — but it can also be extremely complex to get started and thrive. The SBA and its resource partners can help you determine if your business is ready for federal contracting by assessing your business for: Marketability​Structure and experience​Systems and capacityAbility to find contracts Shelly Gillis is an Outreach and Marketing Specialist with the Small Business Administration Massachusetts District Office. She’s passionate about supporting small businesses and entrepreneurs in the Commonwealth by connecting them with community partners and resources. Formerly with for the US Census Bureau for 13 years, she was involved in both field operations and Decennial Census promotion in the Boston area. She has a background in sales and marketing, having worked as an award-winning sales representative and sales manager with Entertainment Publications in Massachusetts. Ms. Gillis holds a master’s degree in education from UMass Boston and a Bachelor of Journalism degree from the University of Nebraska with an advertising major. title: 2026 Maury A. Bromsen Humanistic Literary Arts Lecture: Ann Patchett
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Author Ann Patchett headlines the 2026 Maury A. Bromsen Lecture. Ann Patchett has been the recipient of numerous awards, including a National Humanities Medal and the PEN/Faulkner Award. Her novel, The Dutch House, was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize. She was named one of TIME’s 100 Most Influential People in the World and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters. Her books have been both New York Times Notable Books and New York Times bestsellers, and her work has been translated into more than thirty languages. More details forthcoming and registration will open on August 22, 2026. The Maury A. Bromsen Lecture Series at the Boston Public Library was established to celebrate authors whose work illuminates the depth, dignity, and complexity of the human experience. In its renewed form, the series will foreground literature that brings individual lives fully into view—work that reflects Maury Bromsen’s vision of humanistic bibliography by exploring how personal narratives, lived experience, and moral imagination shape our collective understanding of history, culture, and community. The lecture offers a space for distinguished writers to reflect on their creative journeys, share insights into their recent work, and consider how storytelling can deepen empathy and understanding in a complex world. Programming at the Boston Public Library is funded through private support. To learn more about supporting the Library, please visit the Boston Public Library Fund's website.

title: Author Talk: Courtney Humphries - Climate Change and the Future of Boston
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us as author Courtney Humphries discusses her new book on the climate impacts facing Boston and the city’s efforts to mitigate and adapt to a changing climate.Like many of the world’s iconic coastal cities, Boston faces potentially severe impacts from climate change. Depending on global emissions, Boston could face several feet of sea level rise this century, which would leave many parts of the city subject to tidal and storm flooding. Precipitation events could become more frequent and extreme, and its already-humid summers could become dangerously hot, with most days over 90 degrees. Today, Boston is a booming city with a growing population, a glittering new waterfront neighborhood, world-class universities and a strong economy. Its future risks and opportunities related to climate change are shaped by the 400-year environmental, social and economic history of the city’s development. Climate Change and the Future of Boston describes how Boston’s history and current context shape future climate impacts and examines the mitigation and adaptation strategies the city has taken. Boston is a leader in acknowledging the problem of climate change; it has set a goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2050, among other climate-related goals. It has also developed science-based climate models and undertaken a robust planning process to identify strategies to protect its waterfront from flooding and increase its resilience to other climate-related impacts. Its mayor has embraced a progressive Green New Deal for Boston emphasizing the need for an inclusive and equitable approach to climate mitigation and adaptation. But the city also faces structural challenges, such as aging infrastructure, historic racial inequities, rising gentrification and income inequality and ongoing political and regulatory obstacles that hinder efforts to adapt in an efficient and just manner. She will conclude with a set of forward-looking scenarios about what the future may have in store for the city and the lessons it holds for other coastal cities struggling with these challenges.Courtney Humphries, PhD, is an interdisciplinary scholar, teacher, and award-winning journalist writing about science and the urban environment. title: Author Talk: Linford D. Fisher — Stealing America: The Hidden Story of Indigenous Slavery in U.S. History
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join author Linford Fisher in a discussion of his book, Stealing America, where he shows that although the first enslaved Africans arrived in Jamestown in 1619, European slavery in America began more than a century before. The enslavement of Indigenous people began in the years just after 1492, ensnaring an estimated three to six million Natives throughout the Americas. Although largely erased from the public consciousness, Native enslavement continued for centuries to become a colossal phenomenon that affected nearly 600,000 Native Americans in North America alone, revealing the shocking truth that American colonizers enslaved Natives in roughly the same numbers as they imported enslaved Africans. From Virginia to California, from New England to Barbados, Stealing America traces the history of Indigenous enslavement and land dispossession, detailing how colonizers captured Natives and often deliberately mislabeled them as Black slaves to avoid detection. While the American Revolution pealed the bells of freedom for colonists, it paved a larcenous trail of westward expansion that subsequently plundered Indigenous land and stole the labor of Natives from nations like the Cherokee, Navajo, Nisean, and many others. “This double theft,” Fisher writes, “was central to the origins, growth, and eventual success of the English colonies and the United States—not just initially but throughout all of American history.” Fisher will weave together accounts of major episodes in American history including early colonization, the American Revolution, and the Civil War with lesser-known stories of Native enslavement and land loss. Fisher upends conventional histories about the nature of American slavery, revealing enslaved Natives in places we have overlooked, including southern antebellum plantations and the nineteenth-century American West. After Congress outlawed Native slavery in 1867, Americans forced Indigenous children into boarding schools and white homes, where they labored under forced assimilation. This practice was not reformed until the latter twentieth century, when Native nations finally secured increasing rights and self-determination. Linford D. Fisher is an associate professor of history at Brown University. The author of The Indian Great Awakening and principal investigator of the Stolen Relations project, he lives in Providence, Rhode Island.
